case_title: State of Haryana v. Krishan & Anr.
accused_occupation: Contractors holding the licence to run a country liquor vend
accused_victim_relationship: Vendor-customer only: the victims bought liquor from the accused's vend; one witness knew the vendor personally. No other prior connection described.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.120B; IPC s.328 r/w s.120B; Punjab Excise Act 1914 s.61(1)(a)
weapon: None mentioned (liquor adulterated with methyl alcohol, used as poison)
evidence_type: Medical (post-mortem, chemical examiner, eye examinations); eyewitness/victim and relative statements; recovery of bottles and records; documentary (licence, seized records); conduct evidence (destruction of stock)
aggravating_circumstances: Mass deaths (36) and permanent blindness (44); greed for quick money; destruction of remaining stock after the tragedy came to media attention; knowledge of methyl alcohol toxicity
trial_court_outcome: Convicted (Krishan and Som Nath) of IPC s.302 r/w s.120B: life imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine each; s.328 r/w s.120B: 5 years and Rs.5,000 fine each; Excise Act s.61(1)(a): six months RI and Rs.1,000 fine; sentences concurrent. Other accused acquitted.
high_court_outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions of the respondents set aside (acquittal); State directed to pay Rs.2,00,000 to heirs of each of 36 deceased and Rs.1,50,000 to each person rendered blind
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 r/w s.120B (murder by conspiracy); IPC s.328 r/w s.120B; Punjab Excise Act s.61(1)(a), as restored from the trial court
neutral_facts: In December 1980, a large number of people who had bought country liquor from a single licensed liquor vend in a village and consumed it fell seriously ill. Thirty-six of them died and forty-four lost their eyesight permanently. Post-mortem examinations of the deceased found methyl alcohol in their viscera. Doctors who examined the surviving victims attributed their loss of vision to intake of methyl alcohol. Statements made by the victims immediately after they fell ill, and by close relatives of the deceased, consistently identified the vend as the source of the liquor. Police produced and sealed bottles of the liquor from victims, and after the accused were interrogated they recovered empty bottles and corks used for preparing and storing the liquor. The vend's records were seized and were found to have been forged. The prosecution case was that the accused, as contractors of the licensed vend, adulterated liquor with methyl alcohol and sold it through their agents, knowing its toxic effect. After the tragedy received media coverage, the accused's staff were said to have thrown remaining bottles into a river and canal. Some bottles recovered from the canal were not tested for methyl alcohol, and the investigation was criticised for lapses.
physical_harm: 36 deaths from methyl alcohol poisoning; 44 persons permanently lost eyesight. (Para 14 of the judgment elsewhere refers to 44 deaths, which conflicts with the other figures.)
number_of_offences: 4 charged/convicted (IPC ss.302, 328, 120B; Punjab Excise Act s.61(1)(a)); 4 finally upheld by restoration of trial court conviction
premeditation_planning: Yes: Court described the sale as planned and found the respondents knew the liquor contained methyl alcohol and its consequences
motive: Greed for quick and easy money (accepted by the Court)
key_evidence_accepted: Post-mortem and chemical examiner reports showing methyl alcohol; 25+ doctors' identical opinion on causation; contemporaneous victim and relative statements that liquor came from the respondents' vends; testimony of PW-43, PW-44, PW-81, PW-220, PW-225; recovery of sealed bottles and forged vend records; seizure of the licence record; conduct in throwing away stock
witness_credibility: Medical witnesses found credible and consistent; contemporaneous statements of victims and relatives accepted as reliable
post_offence_conduct: Respondents and staff threw remaining stock into river/canal after the tragedy became publicised; Court treated this as supporting evidence
trial_duration: offence: December 1980 (deaths between December 1 and December 4, 1980; FIR dated December 2, 1980); trial judgment: August 18, 2000; High Court: May 09, 2006; Supreme Court: June 09, 2017
legal_representation: For the State (appellant): Sanjay Kumar Tyagi, Addl. AG, Dilip Pratap, Kamal Mohan Gupta. For the respondents: R. S. Sodhi, Sr. Adv., Harpreet Singh Sandhu, Satyapal Khushal Chand Pasi, Ms. Aparna Rohatgi Jain, Mahesh Kasana, S. K. Dhingra
investigation_status: FIR registered (FIR No. 211, Police Station Kalanwali/Baragudha); investigation completed; 48 persons sent up for trial; charge framed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Lapses by police in investigating with the required vigour; no State inquiry into how spurious liquor was sold; High Court noted bottles recovered from canal were not sampled (Supreme Court treated this as a lapse but relied on other evidence)
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted Krishan and Som Nath, acquitted others. High Court: appeal allowed, convictions set aside, compensation directed. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed, High Court acquittal set aside, trial court conviction restored.
prosecution_argument: Not stated in detail; the judgment records only that the parties argued the appeal limited to the High Court's acquittal of the respondents. The State's position was that the conviction should be restored.
defence_argument: Arguments recorded are those made before the High Court: no evidence of conspiracy; no evidence of respondents' involvement or knowledge; no proof that victims consumed liquor from the respondents' vends; no evidence the methanol was supplied by or with consent of the respondents
legal_principle_applied: Contemporaneous statements admissible and relevant under s.7 Evidence Act; cause of death established by medical evidence; individual culpability can be shown without a proved s.120B conspiracy; knowledge of toxic consequences brings the case within s.300 fourthly IPC
precedent_relied_upon: Joseph Kurian Philip Jose v. State of Kerala (1994) 6 SCC 535 (referred to by trial court and High Court); Fakhruddin v. State of M.P., AIR 1967 SC 1326 (relied on by High Court, referred to)
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable: the Supreme Court gave no separate sentencing reasoning and restored the trial court's sentence
judicial_aggravating_factors: Greed for quick money; exploitation of gullible, rustic villagers; scale of deaths and blindness; destruction of evidence after the tragedy
other_sentence_order: Respondents directed to surrender to undergo the trial court's sentence. High Court's compensation directions (Rs.2,00,000 per deceased heir; Rs.1,50,000 per blinded person) not interfered with; amounts already disbursed.
